usamo-usamo-1974-01.title: Divisibility chain
usamo-usamo-1974-01.body:
**Lemma.** For integers $u, v$ and a polynomial $P$ with integer coefficients, $u - v \mid P(u) - P(v)$. Indeed $P(u) - P(v) = \sum_k c_k(u^k - v^k)$ and each $u^k - v^k = (u-v)(u^{k-1} + u^{k-2}v + \dots + v^{k-1})$.

Suppose $P(a) = b$, $P(b) = c$, $P(c) = a$ with $a, b, c$ distinct. By the lemma,
$$a - b \mid P(a)-P(b) = b - c,\qquad b - c \mid P(b) - P(c) = c - a,\qquad c - a\mid P(c)-P(a) = a - b.$$
All three differences are nonzero, and a nonzero integer dividing another nonzero integer has smaller or equal absolute value, so
$$|a-b| \le |b-c| \le |c-a| \le |a-b|.$$
Hence $a - b$, $b-c$, $c-a$ are each equal to $\pm k$ for the same $k > 0$. But
$$(a-b)+(b-c)+(c-a) = 0,$$
while a sum of three terms each equal to $\pm k$ is an odd multiple of $k$ ($\pm k$ or $\pm 3k$), hence nonzero. Contradiction. ∎

usamo-usamo-1974-02.title: Logarithms and a sum of squares-like identity
usamo-usamo-1974-02.body:
Since $\ln$ is increasing, the inequality is equivalent to
$$a\ln a + b\ln b + c\ln c \ge \frac{a+b+c}{3}\,(\ln a + \ln b + \ln c),$$
i.e. to $3(a\ln a + b\ln b + c\ln c) - (a+b+c)(\ln a+\ln b+\ln c) \ge 0$.

Expanding, one checks the identity (for any $x_i, y_i$)
$$3(x_1y_1+x_2y_2+x_3y_3) - (x_1+x_2+x_3)(y_1+y_2+y_3) = \sum_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)(y_i - y_j),$$
because the right side is $\sum_{i<j}(x_iy_i + x_jy_j) - \sum_{i<j}(x_iy_j+x_jy_i) = 2\sum x_iy_i - \sum_{i\ne j}x_iy_j$, and the left side is $3\sum x_iy_i - \sum x_iy_i - \sum_{i\neq j} x_iy_j$, the same.

With $x = (a,b,c)$, $y = (\ln a,\ln b,\ln c)$, each term $(a - b)(\ln a - \ln b)$ is $\ge 0$ because $\ln$ is increasing ($a-b$ and $\ln a - \ln b$ have the same sign). Hence the left side is $\ge 0$, proving the inequality, with equality iff $a=b=c$. ∎

usamo-usamo-1974-02.title: Jensen plus AM–GM
usamo-usamo-1974-02.body:
$f(x) = x\ln x$ has $f''(x) = 1/x > 0$, so it is convex on $(0,\infty)$. With $m = \frac{a+b+c}3$ and $g = \sqrt[3]{abc}$, Jensen gives
$$\tfrac13(a\ln a+b\ln b+c\ln c) \ge m\ln m \ge m\ln g,$$
the second step by AM–GM ($m\ge g$) and $m > 0$. Multiply by $3$: $\sum a\ln a \ge (a+b+c)\cdot\tfrac13\ln(abc)$, and exponentiate. ∎

usamo-usamo-1974-03.title: Reflect one endpoint
usamo-usamo-1974-03.body:
Let the center be the origin $O$, and let the curve join $A$ and $B$ with $|A| = |B| = 1$.

If $B = -A$, the curve has length at least $|AB| = 2$, contrary to the hypothesis. So $A + B \ne 0$; let $\vec m = \frac{A+B}{|A+B|}$ and let $\Pi$ be the plane through $O$ perpendicular to $\vec m$. We show that every point $X$ of the curve satisfies $X\cdot\vec m > 0$; then the curve lies in the hemisphere (half-ball) on that side of $\Pi$.

**Endpoints.** $A\cdot(A+B) = 1 + A\cdot B > 0$ since $A\cdot B > -1$ (as $B\ne -A$). Likewise $B\cdot \vec m>0$.

**The reflection.** Let $\sigma(X) = X - 2(X\cdot\vec m)\vec m$ be the reflection in $\Pi$. Since $|A+B|^2 = 2 + 2A\cdot B$ and $B\cdot(A+B) = 1 + A\cdot B$,
$$\sigma(B) = B - \frac{2(1+A\cdot B)}{2+2A\cdot B}(A+B) = B - (A+B) = -A.$$

**No crossing.** Suppose some point of the curve has $X\cdot\vec m \le 0$. Since $X\cdot \vec m$ varies continuously along the curve and is positive at $A$, the curve contains a point $C$ with $C\cdot\vec m = 0$, i.e. $C \in \Pi$. The length of a curve is at least the length of any inscribed polygonal path, so
$$\text{length} \ge |C-A| + |B - C|.$$
Reflection in $\Pi$ fixes $C$ and is an isometry, so $|B - C| = |\sigma(B) - C| = |-A - C| = |A + C|$. By the triangle inequality,
$$|C - A| + |C + A| \ge |(C+A) - (C-A)| = 2|A| = 2,$$
so the length is at least $2$ — a contradiction.

Hence the whole curve lies in $\{X : |X|\le 1,\ X\cdot \vec m > 0\}$, inside a hemisphere of the ball. ∎

usamo-usamo-1974-04.title: Compute all three probabilities
usamo-usamo-1974-04.body:
Write F, M, S for father, mother, son, and let
$$p = P(\text{F beats M}),\quad q = P(\text{F beats S}),\quad r = P(\text{M beats S}),$$
all in $(0,1)$ (no ties). "The son is stronger than the mother" means that the father is less likely to beat the son than the mother: $q < p$.

The father has three options. In each, follow the tournament until someone has two wins (at most four games are needed).

**Option 0: F sits out (M vs S first).** If M wins ($r$), M plays F; F must win ($p$), then F plays S and must win ($q$). If S wins ($1-r$), S plays F; F must win ($q$), then must beat M ($p$). In every other branch someone else gets two wins first. So
$$P_0 = rpq + (1-r)qp = pq.$$

**Option 1: F plays M first.**
- F wins ($p$), then plays S. If F wins ($q$) he has two wins. If S wins ($1-q$), S plays M: if S wins, S has two wins; if M wins ($r$), M (1 win) plays F (1 win) and F must win ($p$).
- F loses ($1-p$): M (1 win) plays S. If M wins, M wins the tournament. If S wins ($1-r$), S plays F; F must win ($q$), then F plays M (everyone has 1 win) and must win ($p$).

$$P_1 = p\big[q + (1-q)rp\big] + (1-p)(1-r)qp.$$

**Option 2: F plays S first.** Same analysis with the roles of M and S swapped, i.e. $p \leftrightarrow q$ and $r\leftrightarrow 1-r$:
$$P_2 = q\big[p + (1-p)(1-r)q\big] + (1-q)rpq.$$

**Comparison.** Clearly $P_1 > pq = P_0$ and $P_2 > pq = P_0$ (the extra terms are positive). And
$$P_1 - P_2 = p^2r(1-q) + pq(1-p)(1-r) - q^2(1-p)(1-r) - pqr(1-q)$$
$$= pr(1-q)(p-q) + q(1-p)(1-r)(p-q) = (p-q)\big[pr(1-q) + q(1-p)(1-r)\big].$$
The bracket is positive, and $p - q > 0$, so $P_1 > P_2$.

Hence the father's best choice is to play the first game against his wife. (Interestingly, the answer does not depend on $r$.) ∎

usamo-usamo-1974-05.title: Barycentric lengths and the 120° point
usamo-usamo-1974-05.body:
**Step 1: distances from a point of an equilateral triangle.** Since $M$ is inside $PQR$, we can write $M = \frac{\alpha P + \beta Q + \gamma R}{x}$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma > 0$ and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = x$. Then
$$\vec{PM} = \tfrac{\beta}{x}\vec{PQ} + \tfrac{\gamma}{x}\vec{PR}.$$
As $|\vec{PQ}| = |\vec{PR}| = x$ and $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec{PR} = x^2\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac{x^2}{2}$,
$$a^2 = PM^2 = \beta^2 + \gamma^2 + \beta\gamma,$$
and in the same way $b^2 = QM^2 = \gamma^2+\alpha^2+\gamma\alpha$, $c^2 = RM^2 = \alpha^2+\beta^2+\alpha\beta$.

**Step 2: a triangle congruent to $ABC$.** Take a point $O'$ and three rays from it making angles of $120^\circ$ with each other; on them mark $A', B', C'$ with $O'A' = \alpha$, $O'B' = \beta$, $O'C'=\gamma$. By the law of cosines ($\cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac12$),
$$B'C'^2 = \beta^2+\gamma^2+\beta\gamma = a^2,\quad C'A'^2 = b^2,\quad A'B'^2 = c^2.$$
So triangle $A'B'C'$ is congruent to $ABC$ (SSS). The angles at $O'$ sum to $360^\circ$, so $O'$ is inside $A'B'C'$. The isometry taking $A', B', C'$ to $A, B, C$ takes $O'$ to a point $D'$ inside $ABC$ with $\angle BD'C = \angle CD'A = \angle AD'B = 120^\circ$ and $D'A = \alpha$, $D'B = \beta$, $D'C = \gamma$.

**Step 3: the $120^\circ$ point is unique.** Points $X$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$ with $\angle BXC = 120^\circ$ lie on one circle $\omega_1$ through $B, C$; points on the same side of $CA$ as $B$ with $\angle CXA = 120^\circ$ lie on one circle $\omega_2$ through $C, A$. These circles are different: otherwise the circle passes through $A, B, C$, so it is the circumcircle, and an inscribed angle on $A$'s side subtending $BC$ equals $\angle A$; that would force $\angle A = 120^\circ$ and likewise $\angle B = 120^\circ$, impossible. Two distinct circles meet in at most two points, one of which is $C$. Hence there is at most one point inside $ABC$ (other than $C$) on both, so $D' = D$.

**Conclusion.** Therefore $\alpha = u$, $\beta = v$, $\gamma = w$, and
$$x = \alpha + \beta+\gamma = u+v+w. $$
∎
